title: Adding Event Listeners with jQuery
summary: Shows how jQuery attaches event listeners with shortcut methods (.click, .keypress) and the general .on() method, and how a single selection applies the handler to every matched element without a loop. Includes a small challenge: show the pressed key inside the h1.

concepts.heading: Click listeners with .click()
points: $("h1").click(function () { ... }) registers a click listener on the h1; the function is the callback that runs on each click.
Inside the callback another jQuery call changes something, for example $("h1").css("color", "purple").

Comparison with vanilla JS: to listen on all five buttons you need querySelectorAll, an index loop, addEventListener("click", ...) and querySelector inside the callback, setting .style.color. Watch for typos; the editor's syntax colouring can hint that a function name is unknown.
With jQuery, $("button").click(function () { ... }) is enough, because the selection already contains every button and jQuery attaches the listener to each. No for loop.

concepts.heading: Keyboard events with .keypress()
points: Add an input element to the HTML, then $("input").keypress(function (event) { console.log(event.key); }) logs the key pressed while typing in the box. The callback receives the event object; event.key holds the character or name, such as k or Enter.
To listen across the whole page instead of one input, select the body, or pass the document object itself, with no quotes: $(document).keypress(...). Click into the page first so it receives focus.
(Extra) keypress is deprecated in browsers; keydown (also available as $(document).keydown(...), which the reference repo uses) is the modern choice and also fires for non-character keys.

concepts.heading: Challenge: show the pressed key in the h1
points: Goal: when any key is pressed anywhere on the page, the h1 text becomes that key.
Solution: in the document-level key handler replace console.log with $("h1").text(event.key). It reuses the .text() method from the earlier lecture.

concepts.heading: The general .on() method
points: $(selector).on(eventName, callback) takes the event type as a string and the handler as a second argument.
Any DOM event from the MDN event list works: "mouseover", "click", "keydown", and so on.
Example: $("h1").on("mouseover", function () { $("h1").css("color", "purple"); }) changes colour when the pointer enters the heading.
It is more flexible than the shorthand methods since a single method covers every event type.

task.name: Show the pressed key in the h1
task.starting_point: A page with an h1, five buttons, an input, jQuery loaded before the script, and a keypress listener that logs event.key.
task.goal: Whenever a key is pressed anywhere on the page, display it in the h1.
steps: Attach the key listener to the document, not just the input.
In the callback, select the h1.
Call .text() on it with event.key as the argument.
Reload, type, and see the heading change with every key.
task.expected_result: The h1 always shows the last key pressed.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 19 - JQuery/19.06 - Adding Event Listeners with jQuery

pitfalls: Do not wrap document in quotes: $("document") would look for an element named document.
With .keypress on a specific input, only typing inside that input is detected.
The reference repo's button colours differ (red/blue/purple) from the lecture's purple; it also mixes in a vanilla loop for comparison, and contains an author footer to ignore.

gaps_and_ideas: Lesson 'jQuery events'. Tasks: click on h1; click on all five buttons without a loop; log event.key from a document key listener; show the key in the h1; use .on("mouseover"). Demo: an event log panel listing events fired through .on() for a chosen event name.
